text: Ventaquemada is a town and municipality in the Central Boyacá Province, within the Colombian department of Boyacá. It is located 98 kilometres (61 mi) from Bogotá and 29 kilometres (18 mi) from Tunja, the departmental capital. The urban centre lies at an altitude of 2,630 metres (8,630 ft) on the Altiplano Cundiboyacense in the Eastern Ranges of the Colombian Andes. It shares borders with Tunja and Samacá to the north, Boyacá, Jenesano, and Nuevo Colón to the east, Turmequé and Villapinzón to the south, and Guachetá, Lenguazaque, and Villapinzón to the west. Former names of Ventaquemada include Padua and La Venta, reflecting its historical role as a commercial hub along the route between Bogotá and Tunja, the two most significant cities of the Altiplano. The name Ventaquemada ("burnt sale") originated after the burning of Albarracín's properties. Prior to the Spanish conquest, the area was inhabited by the Muisca, who formed the loose Muisca Confederation, and Ventaquemada fell under the authority of the zaque of Hunza. Modern Ventaquemada was officially founded on December 17, 1777, by viceroy Manuel Antonio Flórez. The town is near the Puente de Boyacá, the site of the decisive Battle of Boyacá during Colombia's struggle for independence, and features a classical colonial house and a statue dedicated to independence hero Simón Bolívar. The Ventaquemada train station has been abandoned for a long time. The primary economic activity in the region is agriculture, with potatoes and maize being the main crops cultivated.
